newsitem.title: UK: Parkinson's sufferer Deng had common brain illness.
newsitem.headline: Parkinson's sufferer Deng had common brain illness.

text.p: Parkinson's disease, which afflicted China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping and was in its advanced stages when he died aged 92, is a common and devastating brain disorder.
Sufferers become stiff and sluggish, develop tremors and eventually have trouble walking or moving because of the uncontrollable twitching of their muscles.
Mental abilities are affected in about 40 percent of cases, and victims in later stages often cannot communicate well because the tremors affect their speech.
Parkinson's is the second most common neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer's, affecting one percent of those over the age of 50.

It is caused by a degeneration of the basal ganglia in the brain, with a loss of dopamine, an important neurotransmitter. Neurotransmitters carry messages between brain and nerve cells and dopamine is known to be important to movement.
Well-known sufferers include U.S. evangelist Billy Graham and U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno. Some doctors suspect that the source of Pope John Paul II's tremors is Parkinson's.
Boxer Muhammad Ali suffers from parkinsonism, a syndrome similar to but separate from Parkinson's disease, believed to have been caused by repeated blows to his head.
U.S. doctors reported last November that they may have found a genetic link for many cases of Parkinson's.

Researchers are looking at various ways to treat it, including injections of brain cells from aborted foetuses. There is some evidence these cells can "take" in an adult, but the treatment is controversial.
Last May Hong Kong's Daily Apple newspaper said China was sparing no expense in keeping Deng alive and mentioned expensive injections that he had to have every day.

Drugs known as monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors are also used to treat Parkinson's, and last year researchers said they found cigarette smoke also acts on the MAO enzyme, which breaks down dopamine.
Smokers are known to have lower rates of Parkinson's, although this did not help the former chain-smoker Deng, whose death on Wednesday night was partly blamed on complications from lung infection.
